# Accurate and well-powered case–control analysis of spatial molecular data

Yakir A. Reshef 1,2,3,4 , Lakshay Sood1,2,3,4, Michelle Curtis 1,2,3,4, Laurie Rumker1,2,3,4,5, Daniel J. Stein 1,2,3,4,5, Mukta G. Palshikar1,2,3,4, Saba Nayar6,7, Andrew Filer6, Anna Helena Jonsson8, Ilya Korsunsky 1,2,3,4 & Soumya Raychaudhuri 1,2,3,4,5

As spatial molecular data grow in scope, there is a pressing need to identify disease-associated spatial structures. Current approaches typically make restrictive assumptions such as representing tissue regions by abundances of discrete cell types and samples by abundances of discrete niches; this risks overlooking important signals. Here we introduce variational inference-based microniche analysis (VIMA), a method combining deep learning with principled statistics to discover disease-associated spatial features with greater flexibility and precision. VIMA trains an ensemble of variational autoencoders to summarize the contents of every small tissue patch in a dataset via numeric ‘fingerprints’. It uses these to define many data-dependent, overlapping ‘microniches’ and meta-analyzes them to identify microniches whose abundance correlates significantly with case− control status. We confirm VIMA’s calibration, power and spatial accuracy in simulations. We then apply VIMA to spatial datasets spanning three diseases and spatial modalities, recapitulating known biology and identifying new spatial features of disease.

Spatial profiling of tissue samples has long been a foundational tool in biology1,2 and is now a pillar of biomedical research3–6. In recent years, the scale and richness of spatial molecular modalities have dramatically increased, and modern modalities now profile scores of proteins and thousands of genes at high spatial resolution7–14; however, this richness complicates systematic analysis, and traditional approaches in cancer15,16 and elsewhere17 have relied on manually constructed scoring systems. This limits discoveries to those that fit existing paradigms and scales poorly as more genes and proteins are assayed. Thus, the development of new computational methods for high-resolution annotation of tissue structures in spatial molecular

data has become an active area of research. Modern methods based on local abundances of different cell types16,18,19, spatially constrained clustering20 and aggregation21,22, spatial factorization23,24, graph neural networks25–27 and others28–30 have enabled identification of granular tissue structures. More recent work has begun to explore the intuition that neural network architectures from image analysis can be built upon to provide powerful and flexible tissue representations31–33. Here, we focus specifically on the question of statistical case− control analysis in spatial data: given a spatial dataset with multiple case and control samples, are there patterns that are statistically significantly different between cases and controls, after multiple-testing

VIMA takes as input a multi-sample spatial molecular dataset of any kind as well as sample-level case−control status and covariates such as patient age or sex. VIMA outputs (1) a tensor of samples by microniches by autoencoders called the microniche abundance tensor (MAT) that summarizes the abundance patterns of different microniches across the samples; (2) a global P value indicating the statistical significance of the aggregate spatial differences between case samples and control samples; and (3) a subset of tissue patches whose microniches drive this association at a specified FDR threshold, with a directional effect size for each patch. VIMA’s results can be represented on a consensus nearest-neighbor graph of tissue patches that can be visualized with Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP). To create the patch fingerprints, VIMA rasterizes each sample, performs dimensionality reduction to convert the spatial markers into a smaller set of ‘meta-markers’ (Methods), and uses a sliding window to convert samples into sets of overlapping, square tissue patches (Fig. 1a). It then uses the patches to train an ensemble of ten conditional variational autoencoders34 (cVAEs) with identical ResNet18-style architectures35 but different initial weights; each cVAE learns one numerical latent representation (the ‘fingerprint’; Fig. 1b) per patch while being incentivized to remove sample-specific effects (Methods). We use multiple cVAEs because independent training runs yield non-negligible variability in latent representations (Supplementary Fig. 1), and combining them improves power and reproducibility (Supplementary Fig. 2). To define microniches, VIMA builds on our previous work in single-cell analysis36. For each cVAE, it constructs a nearest-neighbor graph of the patch fingerprints (Fig. 1c). For each patch p and each cVAE E, VIMA then defines a microniche anchored at p as follows: each patch p’ belongs to the microniche in proportion to the probability that a random walk in E’s nearest-neighbor graph from p’ reaches p (Methods and Fig. 1c). The goal is for patches more similar to p to have higher membership. VIMA uses microniches to compute a MAT whose n,p,k-th entry is the fraction of patches from sample n in the microniche anchored at patch p defined by the k-th cVAE (Fig. 1d). This is analogous to computing cluster abundances, but with many overlapping microniches and with a different set of microniches for each cVAE. VIMA meta-analyzes the MAT across the cVAEs (Fig. 1e) to perform both a ‘global’ and a ‘local’ association test. The global test tests overall association with case−control status, while the local test identifies patches whose microniches drive the association (Fig. 1f). For the local test, VIMA computes the correlation between microniche abundance and case−control status, then uses adaptive weighted averaging to meta-analyze the ten correlations for each patch into a single ‘microniche coefficient’ in units of correlation (Fig. 1e). It estimates empirical FDRs by computing null distributions with permuted sample labels (Fig. 1f). For the global test, the per-microniche correlations are combined into a single aggregate statistic across the entire MAT, with significance again assessed by permutation (Fig. 1f). Both tests can control for sample-level confounders such as demographic and technical variables (Methods). We confirmed type I error control in simulations (Supplementary Fig. 3) and quantified power and spatial accuracy in detecting spiked-in case−control signals in real data (Supplementary Fig. 4 and Methods). VIMA requires no pretraining so can be used out-of-the-box on new datasets and technologies. It requires minimal parameter tuning and has favorable runtime: for the three datasets analyzed in this paper, which contain S = 27, S = 42 and S = 75 samples, respectively, total runtime including preprocessing was ~2 h, ~2 h and ~8 h, respectively, on a single GPU. We have released open-source software implementing the method.

Identifying spatial features of rheumatoid arthritis subtypes using immunofluorescence microscopy data RA is an inflammatory disease affecting up to 1% of the population in which immune infiltration alters the synovium, leading to tissue

correction? One simple strategy is to annotate the samples in such a dataset with a modern tissue-annotation method, use the annotations to cluster regions of tissue into ‘niches’ with similar biology, and then to test for differential abundance of the niches in cases versus controls; however, while this approach has been used successfully to find case− control associations16,19,21,22,32, it may be under-powered if the tissue annotation is not sufficiently expressive, if the case−control differences are obfuscated by the hard clustering step, or if the tissue annotation is too sensitive to sample-specific idiosyncrasies. To address this challenge, we introduce variational inference-based microniche analysis (VIMA), a method for statistical case−control analysis of spatial molecular data. VIMA uses neural network-based techniques from image processing to learn compact, informative ‘fingerprints’ for each of many small tissue patches in a spatial dataset, similarly to some recent methods32,33; however, VIMA introduces three innovations. First, it uses a conditional variational autoencoder (cVAE) architecture designed to learn fingerprints that are minimally influenced by sample- or batch-specific effects, thereby enhancing sensitivity to true case−control signals. Second, VIMA leverages the stochasticity of neural network optimization by training an ensemble of cVAEs rather than just one, resulting in multiple representations that can capture complementary aspects of the same dataset while also increasing replicability. Third, rather than using the fingerprints to cluster the tissue patches into discrete groups, VIMA instead defines many small, potentially overlapping groups of highly similar tissue patches, which we term microniches, and quantifies the abundance of each microniche in each sample. VIMA then performs statistical tests to identify nontrivial correlations between the abundances of the microniches and case−control status, meta-analyzing across the ensemble of cVAEs. VIMA produces both a global statistical test for the presence of any case−control difference in the spatial data as well as a local statistical test identifying the set of specific patches explaining that difference at a given false discovery rate (FDR) threshold. VIMA can be applied to any spatially resolved molecular technology, is well powered even at the modest sample sizes typical of research cohorts, and avoids traditional, parameter-intensive preprocessing steps such as cell segmentation, clustering of cells into discrete cell types, or clustering of tissue regions into discrete niches. VIMA produces properly calibrated P values and so can be used for statistical hypothesis testing, a fact that we confirm in simulations. We apply VIMA to three spatial molecular case−control datasets containing four case−control signals and generated with three different technologies in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) (seven-marker immunofluorescence microscopy), ulcerative colitis (UC) (52-marker CODEX) and dementia (140-gene MERFISH). In each case, VIMA identifies spatial features that differ significantly between cases and controls and that both recapitulate known biology and provide new insights. We also benchmark VIMA against seven state-of-the-art methods and find that most of VIMA’s signals are not detectable with these methods. Finally, we show, using an ablation study, that each new component of VIMA is necessary for its performance.

Results Overview of methods VIMA is based on three central concepts. First, we use a deep-learning architecture common in image analysis (augmented to account for sample-specific spatial artifacts) to represent each tissue patch in a dataset with a numerical ‘fingerprint’ summarizing its essential biology. Second, we take advantage of the stochasticity of neural network training to generate ten sets of these fingerprints, increasing our sensitivity to underlying biology, while simultaneously improving replicability. Third, rather than using the fingerprints to cluster tissue patches into discrete, nonoverlapping groups, we instead define many small, overlapping groups of highly similar tissue patches called ‘microniches’ that form the basic unit of association testing.

We applied VIMA to a seven-marker immunofluorescence (IF) microscopy dataset of S = 27 synovial biopsies from N = 22 patients with RA collected by the Accelerating Medicines Partnership Rheumatoid Arthritis and Systemic Lupus Erythematosus consortium38 (Supplementary Table 1 shows the list of markers profiled). The original publication used a larger cohort (N = 70) with ~20,000 genes profiled by single-cell RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) to group the samples into six ‘cell-type abundance phenotypes’ (CTAPs). Given the limited size of the smaller IF cohort, we grouped CTAPs into three fibroblast-rich ‘stromal’ types and three T/B/myeloid-rich ‘immune’ types. This grouping was motivated by the emerging role of fibroblasts in RA39,40 and their association with poor treatment response38. Before using VIMA to test for association to stromal versus immune status, we first evaluated its patch fingerprints and microniches. The autoencoders reconstructed tissue patches with an average mean-squared error of 0.57, improving over baselines of 1.00 (guessing dataset-wide average for all pixels) and 0.75 (guessing patch-average expression). Figure 2a shows an example reconstruction from a single cVAE. The fingerprints also effectively accounted for sample-specific

idiosyncrasies: we quantified local sample mixing using perplexity across samples of each patch’s fingerprint-based nearest neighbors. VIMA produced substantially higher perplexities than other methods, including neural network-based methods (Fig. 2b and Methods). Because this dataset lacks cell segmentation, we benchmarked only three of seven methods; the others require segmented cells and are evaluated in subsequent datasets. On visual inspection, microniches generated by VIMA’s autoencoders exhibit consistent biological features (Fig. 2c). In one arbitrarily selected autoencoder, we observed microniches containing: broad CD34-high staining with interspersed CLIC5-high areas, likely representing CD34+/CD90− sublining fibroblasts near lining fibroblasts; large CLIC5-high, CD34-low regions indicative of lining fibroblasts; CLIC5-high areas with blurred texture and interspersed 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI); boundaries between CLIC5-high and CLIC5-low/DAPI-high regions; DAPI saturation likely reflecting artifact; DAPI-high infiltrates surrounding CD34-high regions that are likely blood vessels; and perivascular CD90-high staining representing pericytes or CD90+ fibroblasts. We next asked whether VIMA could ‘rediscover’ the stromal versus immune distinction found in the larger single-cell cohort, without previous labels. We applied principal-component analysis (PCA) to the MAT and found that sample loadings along the first two principal components (PCs) nearly perfectly separate stromal samples from immune samples (Fig. 3a). Thus, despite using only seven markers from 22 donors (rather than ~20,000 genes from 70 donors in the original analysis), VIMA leverages spatial information to reveal this important source of biological variation. We then applied VIMA’s local and global tests to compare stromal and immune samples. VIMA identified a strong case−control difference (P = 2.0 × 10−4) with 5,222 of 10,345 patches significant at FDR 10% (Fig. 3b). Reassuringly, stromal-associated patches were higher in CLIC5 (a marker of lining fibroblasts) and the immune-associated patches were higher in CD3 (T cells), CD68 (macrophages) and DAPI (nucleated cells; Supplementary Fig. 5), recapitulating expected biology. In contrast, we did not detect this immune-versus-stromal difference using discrete tissue annotations from other benchmarked methods (Fig. 3c and Methods). We next examined the spatial distribution of the VIMA-annotated stromal and immune patches within each sample. Although each sample received a single overall label from the nonspatial single-cell data, immune-labeled samples often contained both stromal- and immune-like regions that were spatially segregated (Fig. 3d). Thus, synovial cells form spatially organized communities with distinct biology not captured by sample-wide cell-type abundances. This spatial characterization advances our understanding of how spatial interactions

among cell types contribute to this disease and challenges the notion of a single disease subtype per patient, with possible implications for precision medicine in RA. We also found biological heterogeneity among stromal- and immune-associated patches. Using Leiden clustering41 on patch fingerprints, we grouped immune-associated patches into two subtypes (Fig. 3e and Methods): one highly cellular, with strong DAPI staining and a T cell infiltrate (Fig. 3e (cluster 1) and Supplementary Fig. 6), and another with spatially proximal CD68-high (macrophage) and CD90-high (sublining fibroblast) regions with T cell aggregates (Fig. 3e (cluster 2) and Supplementary Fig. 6). Similarly, stromal-associated patches formed two subtypes (Fig. 3f): one with strong CD34 staining (sublining fibroblasts and/or endothelial cells; Fig. 3f (cluster 3) and Supplementary Fig. 7) and another with strong CLIC5 staining (lining fibroblasts; Fig. 3f (cluster 4) and Supplementary Fig. 7). We found strong associations between these clusters and two of the six original disease subtypes (the CTAPs). Among immune-associated clusters, cluster 1 was more prevalent than cluster 2 in the ‘myeloid’ (M) CTAP (log odds ratio (OR) 0.73, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.95) and less prevalent in the ‘T cell/myeloid’ (TM) CTAP (log OR −0.91, 95% CI −1.18 to −0.65; Fig. 3g). Among stromal-associated clusters, cluster 3 was more prevalent than cluster 4 in the M CTAP (log OR 1.16, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.65) and less prevalent in the TM CTAP (log OR −2.07, 95% CI −3.01 to −1.13; Fig. 3h). Other CTAPs showed no enrichment (Supplementary Fig. 8). These results suggest that the M CTAP is characterized by vascularization, macrophage−sublining fibroblast interactions and separate T cell aggregates, whereas the TM CTAP has an expanded lining and an as-yet uncharacterized immune infiltrate linked to T cell activation. Identifying effects of TNF inhibition on lymphoid aggregates in ulcerative colitis using CODEX data UC is a chronic inflammatory disease of the colonic mucosa causing diarrhea, abdominal pain and rectal bleeding42. Inhibition of tumor necrosis factor (TNF) has become a cornerstone of treatment42, but response varies and its molecular determinants remain unclear43. To identify the spatial consequences of TNF inhibition, we applied VIMA to a 52-marker CODEX8 dataset of S = 42 colonic biopsies from N = 34 patients (29 with UC and 5 healthy)19 (Supplementary Table 2 shows a list of profiled markers). We first used VIMA to distinguish UC from healthy samples and found a strong association (global P = 1.7 × 10−3) with 11,839 of 21,359 patches significant at FDR 10% (4,146 UC-associated, 7,693 healthy-associated; Fig. 4a). UC-associated patches localized deep to epithelial layers, consistent with known disease biology44,45 (Fig. 4b), and showed higher levels of immune markers including CD3 (T cells), CD19 (B cells) and CD45 (immune cells; Fig. 4c). Unlike with the RA case−control analysis, the UC-versus-healthy signal was also detectable using tissue annotations generated using UTAG21 and post-Harmony46 patchwide average expression profile (Fig. 4d), though VIMA achieved substantially higher statistical significance. In addition, VIMA was the only method that detected UC-associated patches and not just healthy-associated patches, enabling analysis of TNF inhibition effects in diseased tissue (Fig. 4e). We focused subsequent analyses on these 4,146 UC-associated patches detected by VIMA. To study TNF inhibition effects, we used VIMA to conduct case− control analysis within UC-associated patches, comparing patients treated with TNF inhibition in the past (‘prior/chronicTNFi’) to patients with either no TNF inhibition at all or recent TNF inhibition only (‘never/newTNFi’; Methods). We found a strong association (global P = 1.5 × 10−3) with 2,307 of the 4,146 patches significant at FDR 10% (Fig. 4f). Subclustering the UC-associated patches into two clusters (Methods) and comparing abundances yielded similar results (P = 5.6 × 10−3 by t-test; Supplementary Fig. 9), with one cluster strongly enriched for positively associated patches and the other for negatively associated patches (Supplementary Fig. 10). The fraction of associated patches per sample further stratified patients by TNF exposure in a dose-response-like gradient, ranging from longstanding TNF inhibition to previous (but not current) TNF inhibition, recent initiation of TNF inhibition and finally no TNF inhibition (Fig. 4g). Prior/chronicTNFi-associated patches shared features with both healthy and UC tissue: they showed lower levels of B and T cell markers, similar to healthy-associated patches, but higher fibroblast, macrophage and mesenchymal markers (CD54, CD90, CD34 and MMP12; Fig. 4h), similar to UC-associated patches (Fig. 4c). Comparing microniche coefficients confirmed this signal (Supplementary Fig. 11). Spatially, never/newTNFi-associated patches exhibited B cell aggregates with surrounding T cells, consistent with lymphoid aggregates, whereas chronic/priorTNFi-associated patches showed a spatially disorganized pattern of mesenchymal markers intermixed with scant lymphocytes (Fig. 4i). These findings suggest TNF inhibition remodels colonic architecture (potentially in a long-lasting way) by reducing lymphoid aggregates and increasing mesenchymal and fibroblast activity. Our results extend previous analysis of this dataset19, which used a cell-type-based workflow requiring segmentation, cell-type annotation and clustering of spatial regions into ‘cellular neighborhoods’. In a subgroup of UC with intermediate-grade colonic inflammation, this strategy identified a modest negative association (P < 0.01) between TNF inhibition and a lymphoid aggregate-associated neighborhood, but this was limited to one patient subset and was not corrected for multiple testing across patient subsets and cellular neighborhoods. In contrast, VIMA identifies a robust reduction in lymphoid structures in

TNF-treated patients without segmentation, cell-type annotation, or patient subset selection, providing stronger evidence that TNF inhibition disrupts lymphoid aggregation in colonic tissue.

Identifying dementia-associated tissue structures using spatial transcriptomics data Alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause of dementia in older patients47. Single-cell RNA-seq has identified cell populations with altered abundance in patients with Alzheimer’s disease48, but the spatial structures underlying dementia remain difficult to study. We applied VIMA to a 140-gene MERFISH dataset of S = 75 postmortem medial temporal gyrus samples from N = 27 patients48 (15 with Alzheimer’s disease or Alzheimer’s disease-related dementia) containing 516 million transcripts (Supplementary Table 3 contains a list of profiled genes). VIMA detected a significant association to dementia status (global P = 5.4 × 10−3), with 27,072 out of 70,898 patches significant at FDR 5% (Fig. 5a), despite modest sample size compared to the analogous single-cell dataset. The signal was strong: the fraction of dementia-versus-control-associated patches in each sample nearly separates dementia from control samples (Fig. 5b). In contrast, we did not detect this association using annotations generated by other spatial methods (Fig. 5c). A nonspatial analysis using sample-wide cell-type proportions was also null, indicating that spatial information reduces the sample size needed to detect this association (Supplementary Fig. 12). The associated patches map to cortical architecture and reveal both known and new biology. Control-associated patches colocalize very well with cortical layers 2 and 3 (Fig. 5d), suggesting thinning of these layers in dementia and consistent with previous histology49, omics48,50 and neuroimaging51 studies as well as with a nonspatial single-cell analysis of a much larger (N = 84) superset of this cohort48. We additionally confirmed this by annotating patches with abundant layer 2/3 neurons (Methods), observing depletion in dementia (P = 5.7 × 10−4 by a one-sided Kolmogorov–Smirnov test; Fig. 5e), validating recovery of known biology. Clustering dementia-associated patches revealed two clusters localizing to different subregions of layer 6 (superficial layer 6 and the layer 6-white matter interface; Supplementary Fig. 13) and with different cell-type compositions (Supplementary Figs. 14 and 15) but similar associations to dementia (Supplementary Fig. 16). These subtypes may reflect distinct pathological processes. In contrast, the dementia-associated patches identified by VIMA are new. They localize to the deepest cortical layer (layer 6b) but are not uniformly distributed within that layer (Fig. 5d). Compared to other layer 6b patches, they are enriched for oligodendrocytes (1.33× enrichment, P < 1 × 10−4 by donor-level permutation test) and depleted for L6 IT Car3 neurons (0.40× depletion, P < 1 × 10−4 by donor-level permutation test; Fig. 5f and Supplementary Table 4). These differences are not explained by variation in overall L6b neuron abundance (Fig. 5f and Supplementary Table 4). Manual annotation of patches with high L6b neuron and oligodendrocyte abundance (Methods) reproduced the enrichment (P = 1.7 × 10−3 by one-sided Kolmogorov– Smirnov test; Fig. 5g). These results suggest a previously unrecognized oligodendrocyte-rich niche in layer 6b that is more abundant in dementia. Discussion Here we introduced VIMA, a method for statistical case−control analysis of spatial molecular data across a range of modalities, from low-content proteomics through spatial transcriptomics. VIMA uses an ensemble of conditional variational autoencoders to extract numerical fingerprints for each patch of tissue in a dataset that summarize the biology of that patch, then defines overlapping groups of similar patches (‘microniches’), and finally tests whether their abundance correlates with case− control status. VIMA outputs (1) a tensor of samples by microniches by autoencoders called the MAT summarizing the abundance patterns of different microniches across the samples; (2) a global P value for association to case−control status; and (3) a subset of associated patches at

a specified FDR, with effect sizes. VIMA accounts for sample-specific artifacts, supports covariates, requires minimal parameter tuning, and runs efficiently even on datasets with hundreds of millions of transcripts. VIMA is different from the deep-learning-based methods popular in digital pathology56,57, which typically are trained on thousands or even millions of patient samples and focus on patient-level prediction of disease status rather than defining disease-associated spatial structures at specified FDRs in small research cohorts. We applied VIMA to three datasets across distinct spatial modalities and identified new biological signals, including detailed characterization of RA disease subtypes and spatial heterogeneity of rheumatoid arthritis synovium, a spatial signature of TNF inhibition in UC, and a new dementia-associated tissue niche in postmortem brain samples. Benchmarking showed these signals are largely undetectable using tissue representations from current state-of-the-art methods. Ablation studies further demonstrated that VIMA’s key ingredients (rich patch representations, avoidance of sample-specific bias and microniche-based sample representations) are all required for its performance. In benchmarking, we used each tissue representation to cluster spatial units into ‘niches’ then tested each niche for association with multiple-testing correction (Supplementary Fig. 21). Variations on this strategy, such as testing the clusters with a global test statistic akin to VIMA’s global test, cross-sample harmonization or using the representations in a VIMA-like microniche framework, yielded only modest improvements, with VIMA retaining superior performance (Supplementary Figs. 22–24). Thus, both the way patch fingerprints are constructed and the way they are used are important for VIMA’s performance. We emphasize, however, that most benchmarked methods were designed for tissue annotation rather than case−control analysis and perform well for that purpose. Our benchmarking does not assess annotation accuracy within samples, but rather the extent to which such representations support inter-sample case−control analysis, focusing on metrics such as perplexity, power to detect case−control differences and number of significant patches identified. VIMA treats spatial data as images without requiring segmentation into cells, cell types and tissue regions. This enables use across spatial modalities, avoids error-prone discretization and reduces user-dependent parameter choices (for example, number of cell types and tolerance of cell segmentation). It also facilitates simple integration of modalities if available by concatenating marker or gene channels. As this approach develops, incorporating pretrained models,

VIMA differs from many deep-learning-based methods for spatial data by using a variational autoencoder rather than contrastive-learning-based or transformer-based architectures. We chose this simpler framework to keep training time low and to allow us to explicitly incentivize removal of sample-specific technical artifacts without explicitly enumerating what those artifacts are as is the case with contrastive-learning frameworks; however, we hope and expect that future work will reveal architectures better suited for case−control analysis than what we have chosen here. While developing VIMA, we observed that cVAEs trained on the same data produce variable representations due to stochastic training, suggesting that each captures a distinct view of the data (Supplementary Fig. 1). Using an ensemble of ten cVAEs leverages these complementary representations to improve detection of true signal while increasing replicability, with diminishing returns beyond ten models (Supplementary Fig. 2). Because data loading dominates runtime, training ten cVAEs in parallel increases runtime by only ~5× rather than 10×, allowing VIMA’s runtime to stay relatively short despite the training of so many models. VIMA has several limitations. First, although VIMA runs quickly, this requires a GPU; CPU-only use can be slow unless multiple cores are available. Second, dramatically different choices of patch size (for example, 40 μm versus 400 μm in length) may emphasize different types of signals. Third, interpreting VIMA’s results requires downstream analysis; we maintain, however, that as with other genomic modalities this process is always necessary, whether before or after the case−control analysis is performed, and that applying this careful thought after the spatial regions of interest are delineated may be advantageous. In practice, interpretation can be performed using tools such as cell-type annotation, clustering and niche calling, differential expression and marker visualization, and may be complemented by methods for fine-grained spatial annotation such as the ones benchmarked in this study, which could provide biological context for the microniches that VIMA prioritizes. Finally, while VIMA’s flexibility enables detection of diverse signals, targeted methods may outperform it when their assumptions closely match the underlying biology. Despite these limitations, VIMA is a sensitive and accurate way to identify disease-relevant spatial features across a range of spatial modalities by combining deep learning with a rigorous and flexible statistical framework. As spatial datasets grow in size and dimensionality, methods that capture sample-level variation will be increasingly important for translating these data into advances in our understanding of disease.

Methods Variational inference-based microniche analysis Intuition. VIMA is built on two technical concepts: (1) the patch fingerprint, which is a numerical representation of a tissue patch learned by a variational autoencoder that can be used to quantitatively assess the similarity of pairs of patches; and (2) the microniche, which is a small set of tissue patches from multiple samples that are biologically very similar to each other. Broadly, our method proceeds by using the patch fingerprints to construct the microniches and then finding case−control differences by searching for microniches whose abundance correlates with case status in a statistical hypothesis testing framework. In this section, we first establish notation, then describe preprocessing (including pixel-level batch correction), patch fingerprint extraction via conditional variational autoencoders, microniche construction for each autoencoder and statistical association testing with meta-analysis across autoencoders.

Notation and assumptions. Let {S1, ⋯, SN} be a set of N spatial molecular samples with M different markers or genes measured for each sample. We assume that each sample has been rasterized into pixels of size r x r, and we represent each sample SN as a tensor of shape (Xn, Yn, M) whose (x, y, m)-th entry is either the intensity of marker m in the x,y-th pixel (for nontranscript-based modalities) or the total count of gene m in the x,y-th pixel (for transcript-based modalities). For ease of exposition, we occasionally refer below to this number as intensity even for transcript-based modalities. In all analyses in this paper, we set r to be 10 μm; however, smaller values are in principle possible and could reveal aspects of tissue architecture that occur on smaller length scales.

Preprocessing and pixel-level batch correction. VIMA pre-processes data to (1) separate tissue from background; (2) reduce a potentially large number of markers into a more manageable set of ‘meta-markers;’ and (3) remove sample- or batch-specific artifacts. To accomplish (1), we summarize the total amount of signal in each pixel in a modality-dependent way, for example, using the total number of transcripts in that pixel (for transcript-based modalities) or the sum of all marker intensities divided by the sum of the intensities of all negative control stains (for nontranscript-based modalities). VIMA then uses this number to segment each slide into foreground (tissue) and background. For transcript-based modalities, VIMA simply applies a threshold of ten transcripts per pixel. For nontranscript-based modalities, in which nonspecific background staining is a prominent feature, VIMA instead uses Otsu thresholding58. Once the foreground is defined, all background pixel intensities are set to 0 for all markers. To accomplish (2), VIMA log-normalizes non-empty pixels using the dataset-wide median total intensity, then averages values within a 5 × 5 neighborhood to form ‘meta-pixels.’ PCA is performed on these to obtain loadings across markers. These loadings are then applied to the original (unsmoothed) pixels to generate K-dimensional meta-marker representations (default K = 10, or K = 5 when fewer markers are available). To accomplish (3), VIMA removes sample-specific and batchspecific artifacts by applying the Harmony algorithm46 with default parameters to the meta-marker representation of all the non-empty pixels in the dataset.

(Depending on cellular density, each tissue patch typically contains tens to hundreds of cells. As the tissue patches overlap, a 1 × 1-cm tissue fragment would yield 10,000 tissue patches with meta-marker information on 1 million pixels.) All patches for which fewer than 20% of the pixels contain tissue (as opposed to background) are then discarded.

Definition of microniches. Once the autoencoders are trained, they are each run on all P patches in the dataset whose tissue density (the fraction of pixels containing tissue) is greater than some threshold α to produce a C-dimensional vector zp for each patch p; α is set to 0.5 by default. Each set of embeddings zp is then used to construct a nearest-neighbor graph of all P patches using scanpy’s neighbors function61. The microniches are then defined similarly to how transcriptional neighborhoods are defined in our previous work in nonspatial single-cell analysis36. Non-null simulations To assess the power and spatial accuracy of VIMA, we downsampled the SEA-AD dementia cohort to just the samples that had at least 100 tissue patches that passed VIMA’s transcript-density-based quality control filter, choosing for each donor the sample with the most patches if multiple samples met this criterion for a single donor. This resulted in a set of S = 21 samples (with unique donors). We then created a case-associated tissue structure by arbitrarily choosing a 400 × 400-μm tissue patch from one of the samples and increasing the value of the second harmonized meta-marker in all pixels by 2 s.d. We then simulated two types of signals: (1) a ‘case-only’ signal, in which control samples were left unmodified and a tunable number of copies of this tissue structure, with Gaussian noise added to each pixel, were spiked into each case sample in random locations; and (2) an ‘enrichment’ signal, in which a fixed number of copies of this tissue structure, with Gaussian noise added to each pixel, were spiked into each case sample in random locations and a smaller but nonzero number were similarly spiked into each control sample at a specified, tunable ratio of abundance between cases and controls. For each signal, we generated 30 simulates at a number of different signal strengths determined either by the abundance of the structure in cases (in the ‘case-only’ scenario) or the ratio of abundance in cases to abundance in controls (in the ‘enrichment’ scenario). For each signal strength, we quantified power in the standard way at level 5%. We also quantified VIMA’s spatial accuracy as follows: for each simulate, we computed the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve obtained from using VIMA’s microniche coefficients to classify each patch as either containing the spiked-in signal or not. We then averaged this over all simulates at each signal strength. The results are shown in Supplementary Fig. 4.

We assessed performance in non-null simulations using three metrics: (1) power to reject the null at level α = 0.05; (2) accuracy at identifying spatial regions driving case−control differences; and (3) number of significant microniches (for methods i(a) through iv(a)). For (1), we computed power in the standard way. For (2), we computed accuracy by using microniche-level scores to classify patches as case-associated, control-associated or null, quantified using the average of two area under the receiver operating characteristic curve values: distinguishing layer 2/3 patches in cases from others, and in controls from others. A score of 1 indicates perfect separation (case-associated positive, null zero, control-associated negative), and 0.5 indicates no signal. For methods i(a)−iv(a), we used VIMA-derived microniche scores; for iv(b), we used cluster-level t-statistics. For (3), we used the number of microniches passing FDR 10% (not applicable for iv(b)).

Statistics and reproducibility We did not perform a statistical analysis for choosing sample sizes. We assessed reproducibility by computing permutation-based P values when possible, and in the dementia analysis by reproducing the main analysis in random bootstrapped re-samplings of the data. We did not exclude samples, but we excluded tissue pixels if they did not contain enough protein or gene signal, and we excluded tissue patches if they did not contain enough non-empty pixels, as described above. No blinding was performed.
